name: Arjuna's Dilemma
dilemma: Should I go to war against my own family and friends?
context: Arjuna is faced with battling his cousins in a righteous war. His emotional bonds threaten to paralyze him morally.
resolution: Krishna teaches him that duty (dharma) transcends personal attachment. Sometimes the right choice requires acting against our feelings.
lesson: Duty may require sacrifice. Hiding from hard choices is not virtue.

name: Odysseus and the Sirens
dilemma: How do I stay true to my path when temptation is irresistible?
context: Odysseus must sail past the Sirens whose song is so beautiful that sailors abandon their purpose and crash to their death.
resolution: Odysseus had his men tie him to the mast and fill their ears with wax. He acknowledged temptation without surrendering to it.
lesson: Sometimes you must remove yourself from temptation. Awareness is not weakness.

name: Prometheus's Sacrifice
dilemma: Should I defy authority to help others if it costs me dearly?
context: Prometheus steals fire from the gods to give to humanity, knowing Zeus will eternally punish him.
resolution: Prometheus chooses humanity's need over personal safety. His suffering becomes the price of progress.
lesson: Compassion sometimes demands sacrifice. Some things are worth the cost.

name: Filial Piety vs Justice
dilemma: My parent is wrong. Do I obey family loyalty or speak truth?
context: Confucianism teaches deep family loyalty, yet also justice. What happens when they conflict?
resolution: Confucius teaches you must speak the truth respectfully, but harmony (finding the deeper right action) transcends both.
lesson: True loyalty sometimes means respectfully challenging what's wrong.

name: Marcus Aurelius on Duty
dilemma: How do I do the right thing when it's unpopular?
context: Marcus Aurelius, as emperor, could have chosen comfort. Instead he constantly chose duty and virtue despite the cost.
resolution: He accepted that virtue is its own reward. Your only responsibility is your choice and character.
lesson: You cannot control outcomes, only your integrity. That is enough.

name: The Middle Way
dilemma: Do I pursue pleasure or deny myself? Neither?
context: Siddhartha tried extreme asceticism and extreme indulgence. Neither led to understanding.
resolution: He discovered the Middle Way - not between extremes, but a path that balances discipline with compassion.
lesson: The wisest path often transcends the binary choice.

name: The Good Samaritan
dilemma: Do I help a stranger when it costs me time/resources?
context: A man is beaten and left on the road. A priest and Levite pass by. A Samaritan (outsider/enemy) stops to help.
resolution: Jesus teaches that compassion transcends social boundaries. The Samaritan becomes the moral exemplar.
lesson: Compassion isn't about convenience or ideology - it's about action.

name: Epictetus: Master and Slave
dilemma: How do I maintain dignity when I have no power?
context: Epictetus was a slave. His master threatened to break his leg. He could not resist physically.
resolution: Epictetus realized his master could break his body, but never his will or character. He remained unbroken.
lesson: No one can control your mind. That's where freedom truly lies.

name: Wu Wei - Effortless Action
dilemma: Should I force change or align with what is?
context: Taoism teaches non-action (wu wei) - not laziness, but acting in harmony with the nature of things.
resolution: Water doesn't fight the mountain. It flows around it. Yet it shapes stone. Effortless action is most powerful.
lesson: Fighting reality exhausts you. Wisdom means understanding the flow.

name: Hillel's Teachings
dilemma: How do I balance self-interest with community?
context: Hillel taught: 'If I am not for myself, who will be for me? But if I am only for myself, what am I?'
resolution: The answer lies in integration - taking care of yourself while remaining connected to and serving others.
lesson: Self-care and service aren't opposed - they're interdependent.

name: Sartre: Freedom and Responsibility
dilemma: If I'm truly free to choose, how do I know what's right?
context: Sartre argued we are 'condemned to be free' - no God or nature determines our choices.
resolution: With freedom comes radical responsibility. You cannot hide behind rules or circumstances. You must choose.
lesson: Your freedom is your burden and your dignity. Own it.

name: Aristotle's Phronesis
dilemma: How do I know what virtue requires in this specific situation?
context: Virtue isn't a set of rules. Courage looks different in different contexts. Generosity isn't the same everywhere.
resolution: Phronesis (practical wisdom) is the ability to perceive the right action in the specific circumstance.
lesson: Maturity is learning to perceive what the moment requires.

name: The Seventh Generation Principle
dilemma: Who am I responsible to in my decisions?
context: Many indigenous cultures teach that decisions should consider impact seven generations into the future.
resolution: You are responsible not just to yourself, but to those who will inherit the world your choices create.
lesson: Think beyond your lifetime. You are part of a chain.
